title: India and China Just Held Their 35th Border Meeting in Beijing. They Discussed Something New: Delimitation.
excerpt: For the first time since the 2020 Galwan standoff, both sides are talking about drawing the actual border — not just managing the tensions around it.
body:
India and China held the 35th meeting of the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs (WMCC) in Beijing on May 27, and both sides described the talks as "constructive and forward-looking." But what made this round different from the thirty-four before it was the agenda: for the first time since the 2020 Galwan clashes, the two countries discussed the delimitation of the Line of Actual Control.

Delimitation — the process of formally defining where the border actually runs — is a fundamentally different exercise from disengagement and de-escalation, which have dominated India-China border diplomacy for the past six years. Disengagement is about pulling troops apart. Delimitation is about deciding what belongs to whom.

## What Happened at the 35th WMCC

The Ministry of External Affairs said both sides discussed four broad areas: delimitation of the LAC, border management, mechanism-building, and cross-border cooperation including trans-border rivers. The two nations reaffirmed that peace and tranquillity in border areas remain the foundation for gradual normalisation of bilateral relations.

This is significant because it signals that both governments are willing to move from crisis management to structural resolution. The WMCC mechanism was established precisely for this purpose, but for most of its existence, its meetings have been consumed by the fallout from the 2020 standoff — troop positions, buffer zones, and patrol routes.

## The Disengagement Timeline

The shift to delimitation was made possible by the completion of disengagement at all friction points in eastern Ladakh. In October 2024, India and China reached an agreement on patrolling arrangements at Depsang Plains and Demchok, the last two friction points. Prior to that, disengagement had been completed at Pangong Tso, Gogra, Hot Springs, and Galwan Valley.

The Ministry confirmed that the October 2024 agreement has been "fully implemented according to agreed modalities and timelines." Patrolling activities and grazing have resumed as per longstanding practices that existed before April 2020, when the standoff began.

## The Doval-Wang Yi Track

The WMCC talks feed into a higher-level diplomatic track. National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi serve as Special Representatives on the India-China boundary question. Their upcoming meeting — expected in the coming months — is where any substantive progress on delimitation would need to be formalised.

The Special Representatives mechanism has been the primary channel for boundary negotiations since 2003. Twenty-two rounds of talks have been held, producing agreements on "political parameters and guiding principles" for a settlement in 2005. But the actual work of drawing a mutually accepted border has never advanced beyond preliminary stages.

## What This Means for the Relationship

The India-China relationship has been in a state of controlled thaw since Prime Minister Modi and President Xi Jinping met on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in Kazan in October 2024 — their first bilateral meeting in five years. Since then, the two sides have resumed the Foreign Secretary-Vice Minister mechanism, held multiple rounds of military talks, and now advanced the WMCC to its 35th session.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar has described the completion of disengagement as setting bilateral ties "in the direction of some improvement." But he has also been careful to note that trust will take time to rebuild. The 2020 standoff — which included the Galwan Valley clash that killed 20 Indian soldiers and an unknown number of Chinese troops — left deep scars on both sides.

## Trans-Border Rivers: A Quiet but Critical Issue

The WMCC also discussed trans-border rivers, an issue that rarely makes headlines but has significant implications for India's water security. China controls the upper reaches of the Brahmaputra (known as the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet) and has been building dams and diversion infrastructure in the region. India has repeatedly sought a formal water-sharing arrangement, but China has resisted binding commitments.

The inclusion of trans-border rivers in the WMCC agenda suggests that India is pushing for this issue to be part of the broader normalisation package, rather than treated as a separate technical matter.

## The Road to a Border Settlement

A full India-China border settlement remains a distant prospect. The two countries share a 3,488-kilometre border that has never been formally demarcated, and the territorial claims on both sides are deeply entrenched. But the fact that delimitation is now on the WMCC agenda — rather than confined to the Special Representatives track — represents a meaningful expansion of the diplomatic aperture.

For the Indian diaspora, the trajectory of India-China relations is closely watched. Stability on the northern border is a prerequisite for India's broader economic and strategic ambitions, and any progress toward a formal boundary settlement would reshape the geopolitical calculus of the Indo-Pacific.
